analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from forcing workers and consumers into arbitration for employment, consumer, franchise, and civil rights disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past a Senate committee: it sat in the Judiciary Committee for the rest of the 111th Congress and was never voted on.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies today often write fine-print clauses into job applications, credit cards, and purchases that force any dispute into private arbitration instead of court, where an arbitrator's decision is nearly final and there is no public record. This bill would declare such pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, franchise, and civil rights disputes, restoring people's right to go before a judge or jury and to join class actions. It would also require a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid. Clauses negotiated between employers and labor unions would stay in place, except that they could not waive a worker's right to go to court over constitutional or statutory rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, franchisees, and civil rights plaintiffs who are currently required to sign away their day in court as a condition of getting a job, a credit card, a bank account, or a franchise. They would again be able to sue in court, where proceedings are public, decisions are written and reviewable, and class actions remain available. The bill's own findings note that arbitrators face pressure to favor the corporate 'repeat players' who decide whether they get repeat business [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, consumers, franchisees, and civil rights plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no pre-dispute arbitration agreement is valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, franchise, or civil rights dispute [S2][S3].
Requires that the validity and enforceability of an arbitration agreement be decided by a court under federal law, rather than by an arbitrator, regardless of how the challenge is raised [S2][S3].
Preserves arbitration in collective bargaining agreements but bars those clauses from waiving a worker's right to enforce constitutional or statutory rights in court [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that millions of consumers and employees have been forced to give up jury trials, often without realizing it, and that arbitration lacks transparency and meaningful judicial review [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, telecom and retail companies, large employers, and franchise chains that rely on arbitration clauses to head off lawsuits and class actions would face more courtroom litigation and greater exposure to class suits. Private arbitration firms would lose the forced-arbitration business built on those clauses. Businesses argue this raises their costs, which can be passed to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, banks, franchise chains, arbitration firms

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for some disputes, so a blanket ban could increase litigation costs and court caseloads, costs businesses may pass along in prices.

The bill applies to all employment disputes, including high-level executives who have real bargaining power and might voluntarily choose arbitration, rather than drawing a line based on who genuinely lacks a choice.
Opponents of the broader arbitration-fairness effort argued that Congress should not rewrite the Federal Arbitration Act, which courts had long applied to consumer and employment contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside is large and concrete: a real day in court, public records, and the class-action tool that is often the only way to challenge small-dollar ripoffs. The costs fall mainly on companies and arbitration providers, and some of the litigation-cost concerns are legitimate but modest compared with what individuals give up under forced arbitration. The main weakness is design breadth rather than purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never acted, and no vote ever happened in either chamber before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 29, 2009 by Sen. Feingold along with seven other Senate Democrats (Durbin, Kerry, Whitehouse, Wyden, Udall of New Mexico, Merkley, and Kennedy) [S1][S3].
Read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
No further action was taken after the referral: no committee vote, no Senate floor vote, and no House action before the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S5].
Thirteen Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that keep workers and customers out of court through fine-print arbitration clauses, and the private arbitration firms whose business depends on those clauses, because the bill died without any vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms using forced-arbitration clauses, and arbitration providers

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats, no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the floor was never tested.

industries.note: Arbitration firms' consumer and employment business exists almost entirely because contracts force people into their forums. The bill's findings state these firms face pressure to favor the corporate repeat players who decide whether they get repeat business [S3]. The bill would erase that business stream. (Note: this stance reflects the arbitration system the bill targets, not the bill itself, which these firms opposed.)

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer finance companies
industries.note: These companies use arbitration clauses and class-action bans in cardholder and account agreements to limit lawsuits over small-dollar disputes. The bill would let customers sue in court and join class actions again.
Employers commonly require workers to arbitrate discrimination and wage claims as a condition of the job. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable, restoring court access for employees.
Franchise contracts frequently require franchisees to arbitrate disputes with the franchisor. The bill would cover franchise disputes, giving franchisees access to courts.
